Now they're increasingly fearful MS EK Maryana Sych , Ekaterina Kochkina, RFE/RL 2026.08.09 08:00 Ukrainian refugees in Poland. | AP Shortly before she and her boyfriend were brutally beaten on the streets of the Polish city of Wroclaw, a Ukrainian woman named Anastasia Kitsay was inside a shop buying coffee. When another man cut in front of her at the register to buy a beer, Kitsay pointed out there was a line, Kitsayâs mother, Karyna, said. The man responded, âAre you in Ukraine?â and called her a âUkrainian ragâ, as they argued and the man left the store, Karyna told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service. Moments later, the man and two others pummeled and kicked Kitsayâs Ukrainian boyfriend, Maksym, as he stood by his car, while also punching Kitsay. The fight, which took place on July 26, was captured on video and circulated widely in Ukrainian and Polish social media. Both were hospitalised. Two of the men pleaded not guilty to charges of ethnically motivated assault during a July 29 appearance in a Wroclaw court. The cityâs mayor condemned the incident: "There is not and will not be tolerance in our city for violence motivated by hatred, xenophobia, or national prejudice." Since the start of Russiaâs all-out invasion in February 2022, Poland has taken in more Ukrainian refugees than any other European country except for Germany: nearly 1 million Ukrainians had refugee status in Poland as of April, according to United Nations figures. Both the current government in Warsaw and its predecessor have embraced the defence of neighbouring Ukraine as a national-security priority. The Ukrainian population has also helped jolt Polandâs already humming economy. About 1 million are classified as labour migrants, according to Ukraineâs ambassador to Poland. But Ukrainians report growing tensions and resentment from some Poles, who have questioned the depth and duration of taxpayer-funded support for the refugees. Polish police have reported a 30-percent increase in hate crime attacks on Ukrainians over the past six months, according to the newspaper Rzeczpospolita. Refugees in Ukraine | AP 'Speak Polish in Poland!' Kitsay is not a refugee. She said she's lived in Poland for nearly a decade; her daughter Anastasia moved in 2019. But Natalya Melynk is. After the start of the war, she moved from the western Ukrainian region of Zhytomyr to Plock, a city west of Warsaw. On June 27, she said her 15-year-old son and his Ukrainian friend were returning home on a bus when another passenger heard them speaking Ukrainian. "'Polandâs for Poles,'" she said the man told them. âThe children were silent, then he said to my son again: "'You hear me? Polandâs for Poles. Speak Polish in Poland.'" Melnyk said her son speaks Polish well, and he replied that they were speaking Ukrainian because his friend was Ukrainian. "In response, the man started shouting: 'Get off the bus. Get out of the country,'" she told Current Time. After her son said they would get off the bus at his stop, Melnyk said the man lunged at her son, and struck his friend. Another passenger told the yelling man to get off the bus. At the following stop, the man âliterally threw the children off the busâ, she said. Police officers investigated but did not classify the attack as a hate crime until Melnyk complained. As of July 29, the man has not been identified, she said. The rise in reported hate crimes comes as public surveys show Poles becoming less supportive of Ukrainian refugees. A survey conducted earlier this month by the Centre for Public Opinion Research found that 52 percent of Poles opposed accepting any more Ukrainian war refugees; 42 percent said they were in favour. That figure is down sharply from 2022, just after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, when 94 percent of Poles said they were in support of accepting Ukrainian war refugees. The survey also showed that a majority of Poles, steeped in memories of the Nazi-Soviet invasion in 1939 and decades of dominance by the Soviet Union, support restricting free access to health care for Ukrainians, who until recently were not required to pay into the national health insurance system. UPA inscriptions during the 2014 Maidan revolution. | AP Historical grievance The increase in anti-Ukrainian sentiment also comes at a time of strained relations between Warsaw and Kyiv, over a historical grievance dating back decades. In May, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced he would be honouring a military unit battling Russian troops with a designation named after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army. Poland says the group massacred some 100,000 Poles during World War Two, in a region that today borders Ukraine. At the time, the region was under German control. Poland has designated the killings the Volhynian Massacre, and the country's parliament has declared it was a genocide. Ukraine rejects that designation, saying Ukrainians faced hatred from Poles as well, and thousands were killed in reprisals. Ukrainians have termed the events the Volyn Tragedy. Many Ukrainians hail the Ukrainian Insurgent Army as freedom fighters â a perception that has widened as the country tries to fight off a Russian invasion 35 years after it won independence from Moscow as the Soviet Union collapsed. Zelenskyâs honourific designation kicked off a small firestorm of outrage inside Poland. Polish President Karol Nawrocki, a populist historian who is the former director of a World War Two museum, last month announced he was stripping Zelensky of Polandâs highest state honour. Zelensky then returned his award to Poland, as did three of his predecessors as president. "Discussions around the politics of memory [â¦] have once again become a subject of widespread public debate in Poland," said Mateusz Kamionka, a political scientist and expert in Polish-Ukrainian relations at the Jagiellonian University in Krakow. He said economic and social factors are also influencing shifts in public sentiment, including the rising cost of living as well as a belief that public assistance to Ukrainians is too generous and should be more limited. âSpeaking Ukrainian (or Russian) on the street is becoming a problem," said Alexei Cheplyansky, a Polish journalist. "Poles can't distinguish between Russian and Ukrainian. Recently, a Belarusian athlete was attacked with shouts of 'Go back to Ukraine!'" Right-wing political parties are also seeking to capitalise on Polish grievances or resentment, he said. âIt's starting to spill over from the Internet into real life," he added. This story was originally published by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), partners of LRT English. Ukrainian Service correspondent Maryana Sych reported from Lviv; Current Time correspondent Ekaterina Kochkina reported from Prague. LRT English Newsletter Every Friday morning. http://www.bgnes.com/no-filter/us-report.text: BGNES Opinion US Report: Bulgaria Vulnerable to Russian Hybrid Operations US Report: Bulgaria Vulnerable to Russian Hybrid Operations 09.09.2026 - 18:27 Share BGNES The main vulnerabilities include prolonged political instability and polarization, established networks for spreading and amplifying manipulative messages, the capture of state institutions, weak regulatory oversight and low public resilience. Prolonged political instability, deep social divisions, weak oversight and limited resilience to disinformation make Bulgaria particularly vulnerable to foreign interference, according to a report by the US Congressional Research Service on Russia's hybrid warfare in Europe, cited by BGNES. The report, titled "Russian Hybrid Activities in Europe: Issues for Congress," was published on August 11, 2026, by the Congressional Research Service, which is part of the Library of Congress. It cites research identifying Bulgaria as one of the EU countries least protected against malicious information influence by authoritarian states. The main vulnerabilities include prolonged political instability and polarization, established networks for spreading and amplifying manipulative messages, the capture of state institutions, weak regulatory oversight and low public resilience. The assessment was made ahead of Bulgaria's parliamentary elections in April 2026. Anticipating possible interference, Bulgarian institutions took measures against disinformation and hybrid threats and sought assistance from the European Union, the report's authors noted. Bulgaria and Romania are examined together as EU and NATO members in the Black Sea region where Russian hybrid activity has intensified since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. According to the report, such activities could threaten the countries' internal stability, national security and critical infrastructure. They could also hinder the development of Black Sea energy resources and other strategic economic projects. Key threats facing Bulgaria include political interference, disinformation, cyberattacks, satellite navigation disruptions and possible sabotage targeting the defense industry. The report notes that European officials have accused Russia of attempting to influence elections through disinformation, manipulation of social media, illegal campaign financing and efforts to place politicians under its influence. Bulgaria, France, Germany, Poland, Montenegro and Moldova are among the countries identified as targets. Bulgaria has also been targeted by DDoS attacks, in which websites and online services are overwhelmed with massive numbers of requests. Bulgarian authorities and experts have linked such attacks to pro-Russian hacker groups. Systems related to elections, government information networks and critical infrastructure have been among the targets, the report says. Another risk is potential sabotage against Bulgaria's arms industry. The report suggests that companies in the sector may have been targeted in operations linked to Russia. The authors cite investigations and reports alleging the involvement of Russian military intelligence in sabotage and assassination attempts targeting arms manufacturers and people involved in the production and supply of ammunition to Ukraine. The report also examines increasingly frequent GPS disruptions over the Black Sea. In a response to Radio Free Europe, Bulgaria's Defense Ministry said the disruptions were caused by "electronic warfare systems" but did not identify who was responsible. The ministry said information about the systems, how they operate and countermeasures is classified. Such disruptions can pose risks to air and maritime transport as well as military operations in the Black Sea region. Bulgaria and Romania are among six countries examined in detail in the report as targets of Russian hybrid activity. The others are Poland, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia. All are located on NATO's eastern flank, support Ukraine and occupy strategic positions around the Black and Baltic seas. In the broader European context, Russian hybrid activities include sabotage, assassinations and assassination attempts, cyberattacks, airspace violations, GPS jamming, damage to undersea cables and pipelines, the artificial routing of migrant flows, and interference in political and electoral processes. One study cited in the report found that the number of Russian hybrid attacks in Europe quadrupled between 2023 and 2024. Another investigation identified at least 151 suspected Russian operations between February 2022 and March 2026. According to US, European and NATO officials, these activities are aimed at weakening support for Ukraine, dividing Europe and testing the limits of the Alliance's capabilities and resolve without triggering an open military confrontation. The authors stress that responsibility for hybrid operations is often difficult to prove. In some cases, Russian involvement has been clearly established, while in others allegations rely on indirect evidence and intelligence assessments with varying degrees of certainty. Moscow routinely denies involvement in such activities. Following the mass expulsion of Russian diplomats and suspected intelligence officers from European countries, Russian intelligence services have increasingly turned to intermediaries to carry out individual operations, the report says. These intermediaries can include people without specialized training, criminal groups or entire networks of operatives. Some may not even know that their assignments originate from Russian intelligence services. The report outlines several possible actions for the US Congress, including increased assistance to European allies, broader sanctions against Russian intelligence agencies and stronger military, intelligence and law-enforcement cooperation against hybrid operations. The authors conclude that continued Russian activity threatens not only Europe's security but also US strategic interests and Washington's commitments to its NATO allies. | BGNES Follow us also on Watch and Comment news Comment in X More from Opinion How France’s Far Right Is Politicising Animal Protection 23.09.2026 - https://www.bursa.ro/journalists-are-sla.text: The nomination of diplomat Luca Niculescu for the role of Prime Minister, announced in early October, marks the fourth attempt to form a government in five months. The prolonged deadlock weighs on financing costs and Romania's economic credibility. Under these circumstances, the stakes of negotiating a majority go beyond the mere division of ministerial portfolios. Every week lost in the power struggle may come at a cost borne by people who are not part of the negotiations. Consequently, the fear of snap elections can bring political adversaries to the same table-not to become partners capable of effective governance, but to act as negotiators wary of losing their seats, shifting power dynamics within their own parties, or losing control over an election campaign. Should snap elections occur, some political parties could see their support drop even further than in the 2024 elections, while those currently riding a wave of rising poll numbers might find themselves-after the votes are counted-back at the same percentage levels seen in 2024 or even 2020. This uncertainty regarding the outcome is precisely what makes the prospect of heading to the polls so uncomfortable for the leaders of parliamentary parties. *Governance is negotiated in Parliament. "Saviors" are manufactured on television The threat of snap elections has been systematically built up through the media, particularly on TV news channels. Parties negotiate votes in Parliament, but they also negotiate how the public will interpret the deal. Who gave in? Who saved the country? Who committed a betrayal? Who must be portrayed as a danger so that an alliance-deemed impossible until yesterday-becomes indispensable today? An agreement requires a public explanation. When that explanation is manufactured before the actual results are in, television can become the venue where political survival is packaged as national responsibility. Opinion polls also factor into this dispute. Marius Lulea, an AUR co-founder currently at odds with the party's leadership, challenges the image of a party polling at 40%. In an interview with PS News on October 7, 2026, he claims AUR is actually below 25% and warns: "We are lying to Romanians, and we'll end up with 20% in the election." Lulea accuses others of using an inflated electoral profile for AUR-partly to justify the other parties drawing closer together and continuing to govern under the pretext of countering a threat. This is a significant political accusation arising from an internal party conflict. Furthermore, during a recent appearance on the Realitatea Plus channel, Marius Lulea cited studies indicating that approximately 50% of Romanians do not trust any politician or political party. Under these circumstances, how representative is the competition between parties when such a large segment of society-according to this -does not identify with any of the current political leaders? A poll can measure the state of society. However, the way it is commissioned, selected, and presented can influence that very state. A figure repeated night after night on television screens can suggest that a certain outcome is inevitable, that voting is futile, or that a compromise must be accepted out of fear of the alternative. That is why the public needs to know who is paying for the research, when it was conducted, the sample size, the methodology used, and the exact wording of the question. Any political ties held by an institute or its leadership must be made transparent. The label "poll" cannot substitute for verification, just as the existence of a political sponsor does not automatically prove the results have been falsified. *Who pays for the battle for Romanians' attention? The issue becomes even more pressing when these figures intersect with a media sector dependent on political contracts. Data analyzed regarding party subsidies for the entire year of 2024 indicate that approximately 233.1 million lei were spent on media and propaganda. The category extends beyond television-and should not be conflated solely with the revenue of news channels-yet it illustrates the scale of resources deployed for political communication: approximately 98 million lei paid by the PSD, 69 million lei by the PNL, 39 million lei by the USR, and 21 million lei by AUR, according to data from the Permanent Electoral Authority and monthly analyses by Expert Forum regarding political party media spending. These funds were utilized across all types of elections held in 2024: European Parliament, local, parliamentary, and presidential. Documents analyzed by Snoop regarding the autumn 2024 presidential campaign reveal payments made by the PNL to companies linked to Realitatea Plus, România TV, Antena 3, Digi24, and B1 TV. The same set of documents also lists Elena Lasconi's campaign expenditures involving Antena 3 and Digi24. These examples illustrate specific commercial relationships within the campaign rather than the television stations' annual totals. They also demonstrate why the funding landscape is more complex than the simplistic "one party, one channel" formula. In 2025, parties reported spending over 117.6 million lei in state subsidies on media and propaganda, according to Expert Forum. Separately, documents from the presidential runoff campaign show that Nicuşor Dan declared expenditures of approximately 4.64 million lei to România TV, 2.19 million to Antena 3, 1.26 million to B1 TV, and 947,000 lei to the company operating Digi24. During the same campaign, George Simion declared approximately 1.34 million lei paid to România TV and 15.05 million lei to DBV Media House, an entity associated with Realitatea Plus. A Snoop investigation into the 2025 AUR campaign detailed approximately 23.4 million lei directed to Realitatea Plus throughout the presidential election period. This figure encompasses spending across both rounds of the election-or, more precisely, the associated media campaigns. A portion of these expenses was not reimbursed by the Permanent Electoral Authority (AEP), which deemed the rates excessive-a decision that sparked dissatisfaction within AUR and was challenged by George Simion. In this context, Anca Alexandrescu stated: "A private television station has the right to set whatever rates it chooses!" Contract notifications for the current year, analyzed by Expert Forum up to August 31, 2026, reveal-for the *Realitatea* website-a contract with the PSD worth euro50,000 per month (scheduled for February-December 2026) and one with AUR worth euro60,000 per month (for January-December 2026). For *Antena3.ro*, a PSD contract worth euro90,750 per month (including VAT) appears for the period of March-August 2026. A political advertising contract does not prove that every journalist at the media outlet receives orders from the paying party. However, the contract establishes a relationship that the public ought to be able to see. The risk arises when marked advertising, promotional content, guest selection, and editorial judgment become difficult to distinguish from one another. A citizen might watch a program convinced they are witnessing an independent assessment, while the financial ties relevant to that assessment remain off-screen. *Anca Alexandrescu: from PSD communications to Georgescu and the rift with AUR Shifts in attitude among certain hosts make this issue even more apparent. Anca Alexandrescu did not enter the public sphere without a political past. Her CV records work in communications for the PDSR and PSD, as well as collaborations with Adrian Năstase, followed by Victor Ponta, Liviu Dragnea, and Viorica Dăncilă. Her roles in party communications and within the government apparatus during the Dragnea-Dăncilă era are part of her documented biography. This past does not negate the right to practice journalism, yet it is essential for understanding the intersection of politics, communication, and the role of a political talk-show host at Realitatea Plus. Prior to the first round of the November 2024 presidential elections, Anca Alexandrescu raised critical questions regarding the online promotion-particularly on TikTok-of Călin Georgescu: "Where is the money coming from, and who is coordinating this campaign?" Following the results of November 24, when Călin Georgescu took first place in the opening round, Alexandrescu shifted to an ardent pro-Georgescu campaign. This moment is pivotal, as her change in attitude became evident after the candidate-whom she had previously dismissed as a fringe figure-demonstrated in the first round that he could mobilize a massive electorate. We are witnessing a clear shift here, evidenced by the contrast between the questions she posed to Georgescu before the first round and the editorial protection she offered him after the vote. However, tension subsequently arose between the two; this escalated in November 2025 when Călin Georgescu challenged the legitimacy of the mayoral election for the capital, while Alexandrescu continued to back the AUR-supported candidacy for the December 7 vote. Her response was telling: "It's not about the candidates! It's about YOU!" She later stated that she had known in advance that Georgescu would make that declaration. Participation in the mayoral election continued, despite the message challenging the vote that came from the political figure she had previously supported. However, tensions between the two boiled over in the spring of 2026, when Anca Alexandrescu harshly criticized Călin Georgescu-who had appeared on the first of the two broadcasts-during back-to-back shows. Subsequently, she also clashed with AUR during the negotiations for the investiture of the Veştea Cabinet. Thus, on the June 28, 2026 broadcast, Alexandrescu remarked regarding AUR and to his management: "I can no longer support this." This sequence of events is relevant to any political negotiation: a broadcaster's support can build legitimacy, yet it can turn into pressure when the relationship sours. *Călin Georgescu: from candidate to symbol - the voices that amplified his message In the case of Ion Cristoiu, the timeline differs. His favorable stance toward Georgescu was evident prior to the annulment of the elections; it did not emerge merely as a reaction to the Constitutional Court's decision on December 6, 2024. On December 3, appearing on Marius Tucă's podcast, Cristoiu criticized the media onslaught against the candidate: "Everyone is bashing Călin Georgescu; everyone has ganged up on him." Following the annulment, he continued to criticize the institutions involved. Here, one observes continuity rather than the abrupt shift in attitude seen with Alexandrescu after the first round. On December 3, 2024, Marius Tucă and H.D. Hartmann participated in the broadcast where Georgescu presented his message ahead of the second round of the subsequently annulled presidential election. While merely hosting a candidate does not equate to endorsing them, one can track their stance through subsequent commentary. Tucă described the election annulment as a "constitutional coup d'etat." Hartmann later interpreted the vote for Simion as a vote for Georgescu "by proxy." These characterizations helped link Simion's candidacy to Georgescu's political capital and transformed the electoral crisis into a central explanation for the clash between the opposing camps. Following his January 2025 interview with Georgescu, Robert Turcescu spoke of the latter's magnetism, predicting that "He will likely be Romania's president." Turcescu has consistently supported Călin Georgescu over the past two years-a fact recently evidenced by two posts on TikTok and Facebook. Speaking from his hospital bed while recovering from surgery, the journalist-who had previously served as an undercover officer within the media-urged citizens to protest Georgescu's arrest and to denounce the court's decision as unjust and unlawful given the details of the former presidential candidate's latest criminal case. On *România TV*, Dan Diaconescu claimed that Georgescu was "loved by five or six million Romanians," yet in reality, no such numbers ever gathered at any rally or public call to support Călin Georgescu. Over the last two years, the number of people taking to the streets in support of Georgescu ranged from 2,000 to a maximum of 10,000. The statements made by these journalists represent public stances rather than independent measures of popularity. When such assessments are repeatedly voiced by influential media figures, they can help cultivate the image of an inevitable leader. For the public, the distinction between analysis, admiration, and promotion must remain clear. Ionuţ Cristache, the head of the editorial team at *Gândul*-who steered the publication's editorial stance toward the sovereignist camp-offered an explanation himself regarding the willingness to treat certain political groups more favorably. In July 2024, he stated that such support could manifest "through exposure and by limiting criticism," admitting: "I think I was somewhat more lenient with AUR." Yet, in the same commentary, he criticized the promise of affordable housing found in the "Simion Plan." Thus, favoring a political group in certain contexts could coexist with criticizing one of its specific promises. Following the first round of the 2024 presidential election and in the months that ensued, his efforts to defend Călin Georgescu became increasingly apparent, notably through his objections to how Georgescu was being treated by institutions and political opponents. *A shift in tone at B1 TV regarding Nicuşor Dan's decisions A different trajectory can be observed with Radu Buzăianu and Răzvan Zamfir, the hosts of the show *Bună, România!* on B1 TV. After Nicuşor Dan's victory in May 2025, the tone was favorable, with Zamfir linking his election to the valuing of education and performance. By September, however, disappointment was openly expressed. Buzăianu remarked, "This gentleman doesn't seem to be the person we put in office," while Răzvan Zamfir urged, "Remain an honest person even after you've secured the votes." Amidst the criticism, Nicuşor Dan's decision to grant an interview to Mihai Gâdea at Antena 3-marking 100 days into his presidential term-also came to the fore. Subsequently, against the backdrop of the current political crisis triggered by the dismissal of the Bolojan government following a no-confidence motion initiated by the PSD and AUR, two B1TV hosts labeled the president "PSDan." This marks a clear shift in attitude toward him, contrasting with their previous support-which had lasted from at least 2020 through the period following his 2025 presidential election victory. This shift reflects the erosion of the trust-based relationship with the politician they had backed for the presidency and serves as an example of how access to the leader, the choice of interviewer, and the symbolism of an interview becomes a political issue in itself. Such criticism can be legitimate-even necessary. Its credibility hinges on the consistency of the criteria applied: what exactly did the politician do? Which promise was broken? And would the same behavior be penalized regardless of party affiliation? *Sorina Matei and SRS: different histories behind their respective rifts with Băsescu Sorina Matei, too, cannot be defined by a label fixed in December 2024. In 2012, she described Traian Băsescu as "Romania's most powerful politician." By 2015, she was criticizing his support for Elena Udrea, writing that the man who had championed the cause of justice reform had become the "ideologue for those facing criminal charges." Later, her criticism regarding the protocol
